app.caption.listen: Listen to my note. Then it is your turn.
app.caption.paused: We can take a break. When you are ready, I will guide you through it again.
app.caption.practice: Get comfortable. Listen first, then sing it back.
app.caption.preview: Listen to the melody. There is no singing test and your microphone stays off.
app.caption.ready: I will guide you one step at a time. First I will explain and play a note. Then I will listen to you sing and help you with your next try.
app.caption.rest: Take an easy breath. We have time.
app.caption.settle: Get ready to sing. Begin after the soft chime.
app.caption.voiceoff: {description} Listen to the reference, then sing after the soft chime. {tip}
app.choose: Choose what you’d like help with
app.footer: One voice. One small step. No pressure.
app.heard.octave: Your notes seem to be an octave {side} the reference. Match the lesson to that octave, then check that it feels comfortable.
app.heard.score: {percent} of the clear singing I heard was close to the note.
app.heard.short: I need a little more clear singing before I can give useful feedback.
app.hint.high: Let it settle a little lower.
app.hint.octave: Try a more comfortable starting note.
app.hint.off: Listen to your voice. Pitch feedback comes after the round.
app.hint.wait: I only measure your singing turns.
app.how.p1: Listen, imagine the next note, then sing comfortably. Learn a short line before joining the song. Try a little practice regularly, and revisit a familiar line on another day.
app.how.p2: Pitch hints can help you find notes. They are a guide, not a grade for your voice. Try without them sometimes. If your voice is hoarse or tired, rest instead of singing; never push for a note.
app.how.p3: This approach is informed by singing research. VoiceRemedy itself has not been tested in a learning-outcomes study, and a microphone cannot replace a teacher who can hear and observe your technique.
app.intro: No musical knowledge needed. Just your voice and a little practice.
app.options.hints: After a comfortable round, try switching off live hints and listen to your own voice. You still receive feedback afterward.
app.options.score: The score measures closeness to the reference pitch, not tone quality, expression, rhythm accuracy, or vocal health.
app.place.exact: The lesson now starts on that note.
app.place.nearest: The nearest supported start for this melody is {note}. Try a shorter melody if this feels uncomfortable.
app.privacy.active: You can pause at any time.
app.privacy.device: Audio is processed on this device.
app.privacy.idle: I’ll explain, demonstrate, listen, and give feedback.
app.spoken: Spoken coach clips stay in English. The words on screen follow the language you choose.
app.state.finding: Voice check active · follow the instructions below
app.time: {n} seconds left · stop whenever you need to
assess.coverage.detail: We heard some clear singing, but not enough of the planned singing time. Try each turn for as long as it feels easy; it is fine to breathe or stop. Shorter echoes in Gentle pace may help.
assess.coverage.title: Let’s give every note a turn.
assess.great.detail: Most measured singing was close to the target. Keep the same easy feeling as you try a little more independence.
assess.great.title: You’re finding your center.
assess.high.detail: Your typical pitch sat above the reference. Listen again and let the sound settle down without adding volume.
assess.high.title: Let the note settle a little lower.
assess.low.detail: Your typical pitch sat below the reference. Hear it once more, imagine the sound, then approach it softly from below.
assess.low.title: Listen for a slightly higher center.
assess.nosignal.detail: Try a quiet room and a comfortable hum for a few seconds. No score or progress was saved.
assess.nosignal.title: We need a little more clear singing.
assess.octave.detail: Your typical pitch was quite far from the reference. Listen again or use the comfortable-note finder. Do not reach or push for a note.
assess.octave.title: Let’s bring the target closer to you.
assess.steady.detail: Your pitch moved around the center. Try a shorter, easy hum and a fresh breath between turns. You do not need to eliminate natural vibrato.
assess.steady.title: A shorter sound can feel steadier.
chapter.0.skill: Hear a note and answer with a comfortable sound.
chapter.0.subtitle: From “I have never sung” to a note you can find again.
chapter.0.title: Meet your voice
chapter.1.skill: Move between notes and keep a clear vowel.
chapter.1.subtitle: Make small changes with less effort and more intention.
chapter.1.title: Build your control
chapter.2.skill: Sing a simple melody with words, timing, and places to breathe.
chapter.2.subtitle: Learn a melody in pieces, then sing your first complete song.
chapter.2.title: Make it music
chapter.3.skill: Notice how your voice feels and choose rest when it needs it.
chapter.3.subtitle: A gentle finish you can return to after any practice.
chapter.3.title: Leave with ease
coach.answer: Soft as the rain. Let this line settle gently downward. Give each note its own place, then let the word rain finish comfortably. Take a quiet breath before you try again. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.connect: First learn the notes in echo mode. Then choose phrase mode and join them on an easy oo sound. Let the vowel continue as the notes change. Breathe whenever you need to. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.cool: Let us finish gently. Hum softly as the notes step down. Keep your face and neck relaxed, and finish whenever you are ready to rest. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.coverage: We heard some clear singing, but not enough of the whole pattern yet. Let us try echo mode. Listen to each note, wait for your turn, then give it a gentle try. You can breathe between turns.
coach.findoctave: Let us find a comfortable note and its octave. You do not need to know any musical terms. When I finish speaking, hum a relaxed sound near your normal speaking voice for a few seconds. Do not try to sing high or low. The number beside the note will tell you its octave. Then we can move the lesson to suit that note.
coach.five: Listen to the five note pattern. Sing ma on each step at a comfortable volume. Keep the top note easy, and take a breath whenever you need one. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.great: That was nicely centered. You spent most of your measured singing close to the target. Keep that easy feeling, take a breath, and try again when you are ready.
coach.high: Your measured pitch was mostly above the target. Listen again, relax, and let the note settle a little lower. An easy sound is all you need.
coach.hold: Choose a comfortable note. Sing oo, with a loose jaw and an easy breath. Rest whenever you need to. We are practicing steadiness, not holding our breath. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.imported: Let us learn the melody you reviewed from your song. I will play a reference, then listen while you hum it back. Sing after the soft chime. We will learn the notes first, then connect them into a phrase. Keep the whole pattern comfortable. You can adjust the starting note if needed.
coach.joy: Let us learn the Ode to Joy melody. Sing it on a gentle doo, so words do not distract you. Most notes move by small steps. Listen for the longer note near the end of the line. We will join the four lines when they feel familiar. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.joywhole: Let us connect the four lines of Ode to Joy. Listen to the whole theme, then sing it back on doo after the soft chime. Take a normal breath between the lines. If a part is difficult, we can return to that short line. Keep your voice comfortable.
coach.london: Let us sing London Bridge Is Falling Down. Hear the little lift at the beginning, then the steps coming down. Imagine each next note before you sing it. Let the last note finish easily. Learn one short line at a time, after the soft chime.
coach.low: Your measured pitch was mostly below the target. Listen again, then gently bring the note a little higher. Keep your volume easy. There is no need to push.
coach.mary: Let us sing Mary Had a Little Lamb. We will learn one short line at a time. Hum after each reference, then add the words on the screen. Notice the small steps and repeated notes. After a comfortable echo, we will connect the line. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.match: Let your shoulders settle. Listen to my note, then hum softly and try to match its pitch. A small, easy sound is enough. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.melody: Here is my song. Four small words, four gentle notes. Hum the melody first if you like, then add the words. Let the word song last a little longer. You are telling a story with your voice. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.no-signal: I did not hear enough clear singing to give useful feedback. Try a quieter room, move a little closer to the microphone, and sing one comfortable note.
coach.octave: Let us bring the target closer to your voice. Your typical pitch was quite far from the reference. Try the comfortable note finder, or choose an easier starting note. Please do not push or reach.
coach.octavehigher: Your singing seems to be one octave above the reference. That means similar note names in a higher part of your voice. Choose Match my octave to move the lesson up, then check that the new notes feel easy. A microphone can sometimes mistake an octave, so trust your comfort.
coach.octavelower: Your singing seems to be one octave below the reference. That means similar note names in a lower part of your voice. It is not a reason to push higher. Choose Match my octave to move the lesson down, then check that the new notes feel easy. A microphone can sometimes mistake an octave, so trust your comfort.
coach.pulse: Listen for three short sounds and one longer sound. In phrase mode, sing doo on each note. Start when your turn begins. You can tap a finger gently to feel the pulse. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.row: Let us learn Row, Row, Row Your Boat. Feel the gentle rocking pulse. The merry section jumps higher, so choose a starting note that keeps the top easy. We will learn that part in two small pieces. Hum first if the words feel busy. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.sleeping: Let us learn Are You Sleeping. Notice how each little phrase comes back again. Listen for the quicker notes in morning bells, and the lower bell at the end. Keep both ends of the melody comfortable. We are learning slowly. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.song: This is your first complete song. Here is my song. Soft as the rain. Step by slow step. I sing again. Learn it slowly in echo mode, then choose phrase mode to put it together. There are breathing spaces between the lines. Keep the sound easy, and enjoy telling your little story. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.songverse: You have a whole verse to sing. First listen to the complete melody. Then sing the highlighted words after the soft chime. Take an easy breath in the spaces between lines. If a line feels tricky, return to that line in the songbook. Keep the song gentle and enjoy telling its story.
coach.steady: You found the neighborhood of the note. Try a shorter, softer sound, and listen for the center. Let us build steadiness a little at a time.
coach.thirds: Listen for the space between the notes. Sing noo, lightly, and imagine the next note before you sing it. There is no need to rush. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.three: Listen to the three note pattern. Sing oo on each step after my reference. Stay light as you go up. You can always choose a lower starting note. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.twinkle: Let us sing Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. Listen carefully to the space between the notes. Imagine the next pitch before you move. Keep the higher notes light, and lower the starting note if you need to. Hum first, then add the words. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.vowels: Keep one easy note as you sing mi, meh, mah, moh, and moo. Your mouth can move freely. Listen for the same pitch as the syllables change. This exercise measures pitch, not the quality of your vowels. I will say get ready. Sing after the soft chime.
coach.warmup: Let us take a quiet moment before we sing. Soften your shoulders and your jaw. Follow the circle for two easy breaths. There is no need to fill up completely, and no breath holding. You can stop whenever you like.
coach.welcome: Welcome to Voice Remedy. This is a little space for your voice. We will listen, practice, and take it one gentle note at a time.
doc.description: Find your voice, one gentle practice at a time. Offline singing lessons and live pitch feedback.
doc.title: VoiceRemedy · Your singing studio

finder.explain: Listen first. The microphone opens after the explanation. Then hum gently for a few seconds.
finder.explainDone: The letter names the note; the number tells you which octave it is in. An octave repeats the same note names higher or lower. This is the note you hummed today, not a label for your voice. Hear it, check it feels easy, then use it to adjust the lesson.
finder.eyebrow: START WHERE YOUR VOICE FEELS AT HOME
finder.lead: No note names to know and no target to chase. Hum a relaxed “mm” near your normal speaking voice for a few seconds. We will find a starting point, not your full vocal range or voice type.
finder.need: We need a few seconds of a clear, steady note. You can also choose a starting note in your session settings.
finder.title: Find your note and octave.
guide.a.learn: Notice whether you find a note more quickly, need fewer corrections, and remember a phrase by ear. Milestones use repeated pitch results, but comfort, clear words, timing, and expression matter too. The app does not score those qualities. At the end, try singing the little song away from the screen.
guide.a.lessons: Start with a warm-up and your recommended lesson. Repeat it a few times with comfortable breaks. When the notes become familiar, sing the phrase. Finish with an easy hum or quiet rest. Return another day; you do not need to finish the course in one sitting.
guide.a.match: That is a starting point, not a verdict. Use “Find my comfortable note” so the target starts near your own hum. Hear it again, then make a small, slow slide toward it. You do not need to sing louder. If the display jumps, try one voice in a quieter room.
guide.eyebrow: YOU DO NOT NEED TO KNOW MUSIC YET
guide.hear.body: Listen once. Imagine the note before you answer. The letter, such as C4, is just the note’s name.
guide.hear.title: Hear it first
guide.q.learn: How will I know I am learning?
guide.q.lessons: How should I use the lessons?
guide.q.match: What if I cannot match the note yet?
guide.rest.body: Choose one thing from your feedback. Repeat while it feels easy, then connect the notes in Phrase mode.
guide.rest.title: Rest, then try again
guide.title: A little routine you can return to.
guide.try.body: Hum gently when it is your turn. If the line sits low, move your pitch up a little; if it sits high, settle down.
guide.try.title: Try one small sound
help.b1: Begin with the comfortable-note finder, or move the starting note up or down by ear. In Echo mode, the app plays each note before your turn.
help.b2: Wait for “Your turn,” then hum or sing the displayed syllable. Reference notes and rests are never scored. Phrase mode connects notes into music.
help.b3: Finish to get spoken feedback. Each practice ends automatically after its planned turns. Repeat whenever you’re ready.
help.footer: VoiceRemedy 0.2.0 · No account, audio storage, analytics, or cloud processing. Session summaries stay on this device. Pitch feedback cannot assess vocal health, breath technique, or tone quality.
help.more: The female coach is bundled audio, available offline. The speaker button turns automatic feedback on or off. Pitch detection works best with one voice in a quiet room.
help.title: Simple by design.
import.count: {notes} notes · {words} words or syllables. Leave words blank to hum.
import.description: Learn this section of your song, one note at a time.
import.estimate: This estimates a single melody; it does not isolate vocals from a full band. It may follow an instrument. Review the notes before teaching. Rhythm is simplified for practice; lyrics are not transcribed.
import.formats: MP3, WAV and other formats your device can open · up to 15 MB / 10 minutes. A solo vocal or hummed melody works best.
import.label: Your song · {time}
import.lead: Choose an audio file, then a short section to learn. Your file stays on this device. Nothing is uploaded to a server.
import.listenFor: The musical shape of the phrase, with an easy sound.
import.name: Song name
import.placeholder: Leave blank to hum the melody
import.saved: The reviewed notes are saved locally as a lesson. The original audio file is not saved by VoiceRemedy.
import.tip: The melody is an estimate you reviewed. Practice timing is slowed and short notes are lengthened. Keep every note comfortable.
import.title: Teach me my song
import.why: Learn your own song in manageable sections.
import.words: Optional words · one word or syllable per note
lesson.answer.description: Let the melody settle back down: “Soft as the rain.”
lesson.answer.label: Answering phrase
lesson.answer.listenFor: A gentle downward shape with a clear final note. Keep enough easy breath for “rain.”
lesson.answer.step.0: Hear the downward pattern and hum it back.
lesson.answer.step.1: Add the words, one per note.
lesson.answer.step.2: In Phrase mode, sing the whole line and leave a comfortable silence at the end.
lesson.answer.tip: Imagine placing each note on its own step. You do not need to slide all the way down.
lesson.answer.title: Soft as the rain
lesson.answer.why: Descending melodies can drift below the note. Listening carefully on the way down matters just as much as on the way up.
lesson.connect.description: Turn separate notes into one flowing musical line.
lesson.connect.label: Connected singing
lesson.connect.listenFor: One vowel moving through the pattern, with no need to push at the changes. The pitch display alone cannot judge legato.
lesson.connect.step.0: Use Echo mode to learn each note.
lesson.connect.step.1: Choose Phrase mode. Sing the whole pattern on one easy “oo.”
lesson.connect.step.2: Breathe whenever needed. Shortening the phrase is better than squeezing out the last note.
lesson.connect.tip: Think of carrying the sound from one note to the next. It is fine to practice just the first three notes at first.
lesson.connect.title: Join the dots
lesson.connect.why: Connected singing, or legato, lets a vowel continue while pitch changes. Learn the notes first, then connect them.
lesson.cool.description: Come back down with a soft, comfortable hum.
lesson.cool.label: Gentle cool-down
lesson.cool.listenFor: Comfort, not a perfect score. Skip singing if your voice feels hoarse or tired.
lesson.cool.tip: End with ease. If your voice feels tired, skip the exercise and take a quiet break.
lesson.cool.title: An easy landing
lesson.cool.why: This is a chance to notice how you feel and finish gently. A quiet rest is also a good ending, especially if your voice feels tired.
lesson.five.description: Build coordination with a gentle five-note journey.
lesson.five.label: Five-note pattern
lesson.five.listenFor: Keep the top note as easy as the bottom. Lower the starting note if you begin to reach.
lesson.five.tip: Your comfortable range matters more than how high you can sing. You can transpose every exercise.
lesson.five.title: Let your voice wander
lesson.five.why: A five-note pattern gives you a wider musical shape while staying within a fifth. The starting note is adjustable so the top stays comfortable.
lesson.foundation.step.0: First listen to the reference. In Echo mode, each note gets its own turn.
lesson.foundation.step.1: Wait for “Your turn,” then sing the suggested sound softly. The app does not score its own reference.
lesson.foundation.step.2: Take a breath during “Rest.” When the pattern feels familiar, try Phrase mode to connect it.
lesson.hold.description: Give one comfortable note a smooth, even breath.
lesson.hold.label: Sustained notes
lesson.hold.listenFor: A clear beginning and a comfortable end. Small pitch movement is normal.
lesson.hold.tip: Steadiness is about ease, not holding perfectly still. A little natural movement is normal.
lesson.hold.title: A little more steady
lesson.hold.why: A short, steady sound helps you notice changes without using a long breath. Reset with a normal breath between turns.
lesson.match.description: Listen. Hum. Find the place where your voice and the note meet.
lesson.match.label: Pitch matching
lesson.match.listenFor: The reference and your hum feel like the same note. Keep volume easy; louder does not mean higher.
lesson.match.tip: A small, easy sound is enough. Matching a note is a listening skill, and it grows with practice.
lesson.match.title: Find your starting note
lesson.match.why: Pitch matching joins two skills: hearing a sound clearly and finding it with your voice. Start with a hum so words do not get in the way.
lesson.melody.description: Give four familiar notes a meaning: “Here is my song.”
lesson.melody.label: Your first phrase
lesson.melody.listenFor: Let “song” last a little longer. Keep the final consonant light.
lesson.melody.step.0: Learn the notes with Echo mode, using “mm” if the words feel distracting.
lesson.melody.step.1: Speak “Here is my song” in the rhythm, then sing the displayed words.
lesson.melody.step.2: Try Phrase mode. Think about telling someone your song, rather than passing a test.
lesson.melody.tip: Words and pitch are two separate jobs. If one gets tricky, take the words away, then add them back.
lesson.melody.title: Here is my song
lesson.melody.why: A melody becomes a song when the sounds carry words. Learn the pitches on a hum, then add one word at a time.
lesson.pulse.description: Start a soft “doo” when your turn begins, and let it end easily.
lesson.pulse.label: Starting together
lesson.pulse.listenFor: Three short notes and one longer note. Leave a little silence between sounds.
lesson.pulse.step.0: Echo the note until its pitch feels familiar.
lesson.pulse.step.1: Switch to Phrase mode and listen to the short-short-short-long pattern.
lesson.pulse.step.2: Use a fresh “doo” for each note. Follow the moving progress bar.
lesson.pulse.tip: A finger tapping lightly on your leg can help you feel the pulse. The guide shows timing; the microphone score measures pitch, not rhythm accuracy.
lesson.pulse.title: Find the little pulse
lesson.pulse.why: Rhythm begins with knowing when a sound starts and ends. Try the pattern without worrying about volume.
lesson.song.description: Four little lines. A complete original song. Your voice.
lesson.song.label: Here Is My Song
lesson.song.listenFor: Four clear phrases with a normal breath between them. Keep telling the story even if one note is imperfect.
lesson.song.step.0: Learn unfamiliar notes in Echo mode. Use the earlier phrase lessons whenever you need them.
lesson.song.step.1: Choose Phrase mode. Listen to the song, then sing the lyrics as they are highlighted. Breathing spaces are built in.
lesson.song.step.2: After a round, choose one note to revisit. When it feels easy, sing the song again without staring at the pitch line.
lesson.song.tip: Here is my song / soft as the rain / step by slow step / I sing again. Words and music are original to VoiceRemedy.
lesson.song.title: Your first whole song
lesson.song.why: This original song brings together listening, pitch, rhythm, words, and breathing spaces. It is a first complete song, not an exam.
lesson.thirds.description: Find the gentle leap from the first note to the third.
lesson.thirds.label: Interval practice
lesson.thirds.listenFor: Two distinct notes. Imagine the upper sound before your voice leaves the lower one.
lesson.thirds.tip: Imagine the next note before you sing it. Hearing it inside is part of learning to sing it outside.
lesson.thirds.title: Hear the space between
lesson.thirds.why: Melodies contain both steps and leaps. Hearing the destination before making a leap helps you land more accurately.
lesson.three.description: Travel up three notes and gently return home.
lesson.three.label: Three-note pattern
lesson.three.listenFor: The notes move like three small steps, not one long slide.
lesson.three.tip: Think of the notes as little steps. Stay light as you go up, and lower the starting note if you feel strain.
lesson.three.title: One small step up
lesson.three.why: Moving by neighboring notes teaches you how a scale feels. Small movements build the coordination you will use in melodies.
lesson.vowels.description: Keep a comfortable pitch while moving through mi, meh, mah, moh, moo.
lesson.vowels.label: Clear vowels
lesson.vowels.listenFor: The mouth changes shape, but the note stays in the same place. The app measures pitch, not vowel quality.
lesson.vowels.step.0: Start with an easy reference note.
lesson.vowels.step.1: Sing the syllable shown during each turn. Let the jaw move freely.
lesson.vowels.step.2: Listen for the same pitch through all five syllables; do not force a particular mouth shape.
lesson.vowels.tip: You can speak the syllables first, then let them become a small singing sound.
lesson.vowels.title: One note, five colors
lesson.vowels.why: Singing words changes the shape of your mouth. This exercise separates vowel changes from pitch changes.

map.footnote: “Ready for more” means two of your last three practices had at least 75% of measured singing close to the target, with most notes heard and clear singing through at least 45% of the planned singing time. The whole-song milestone also requires Phrase mode. It is a practice milestone, not a judgement of your whole singing ability. All lessons are always available.
progress.empty.body: Finish a practice with a little clear singing and it will appear here.
progress.empty.title: Your story starts with a sound.
progress.lead: A record of showing up for your voice. Saved only on this device.
progress.note: Numbers are a small part of the picture. Feeling more comfortable, listening more closely, and wanting to try again are progress, too.

report.measure.body: “Near target” means within 35 cents, a little over a third of a semitone. Only clear singing during your turn is scored. The reference, breathing spaces, and first quarter-second of each note are excluded. Typical pitch difference: {sign}{offset} cents. Pitch spread: {spread} cents. Natural vibrato contributes to spread; smaller is not always artistically better.
report.measure.feel: These numbers cannot judge tone quality, vowel shape, breath technique, expression, or vocal health. Notice how singing feels as well as how the line looks.
